headline: Never Her Turn
subtitle: Has this country ever had a woman as head of state or government?
stat_label: Woman head of state or government, in her own right
source_name: Wikipedia: List of elected and appointed female heads of state and government. A woman counts when she held head of state or head of government in her own right. Acting, interim, honorary, and governor-general-only spells do not count. Queens and grand duchesses regnant do count. Each country on this board was checked against that list and the officeholder's article.
fun_fact: Italy is has: Giorgia Meloni has been prime minister since October 2022. Spain is has too: Isabella II was queen regnant from 1833 to 1868, and Spain has never had a woman prime minister. Pakistan (Benazir Bhutto, prime minister 1988-1990 and 1993-1996), India (Indira Gandhi), Indonesia (Megawati Sukarnoputri, president 2001-2004) and Turkey (Tansu Ciller, prime minister 1993-1996) are has. The United States is never. An 85-minute acting spell on 19 November 2021 is not counted. Czechia has had neither a woman president nor a woman prime minister. China is left off: Soong Ching-ling was acting co-chair of the state from 1968 to 1972, so China is partial, not a clean no. Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Liberia and the Philippines are also has.

headline: Past Five
subtitle: How far a common finger count goes on one hand
source_name: BBC Future, How the way you count reveals more than you think, 3 September 2021. The country methods are the ones that article describes. Andrea Bender is quoted there on how much finger counting varies.
fun_fact: India counts the lines between finger segments, four to a finger, so one hand reaches 20. China counts to five like the United States, then shows six through ten as gestures on that same hand: six is the thumb and the pinky. The United Kingdom runs from thumb to pinky, the United States from index finger to thumb, and Iran starts at the pinky, so each of those stops at five. The article does not name Pakistan, Bangladesh, Vietnam, Turkey, or Egypt.

headline: Many Clocks
subtitle: How many time zones a country has
source_name: Wikipedia, List of time zones by country. The number is the table's own count of standard UTC offsets. Dependent territories are included, Antarctic claims are not, and daylight saving is not an extra zone. Unofficial offsets count only when the table lists them, so Australia includes UTC+08:45 and China does not include Xinjiang Time. France is 12, not 13.
fun_fact: France has 12 time zones because overseas territories count, and would have 13 only if its Antarctic claim were included. The United States has 11, the same as Russia, once Baker Island and Wake Island are counted, not the four zones of the mainland. The United Kingdom has 9, the same as Australia, almost all of them outside Great Britain. Kiribati has 3, including UTC+14, and South Africa has 2 only because of the Prince Edward Islands. China has 1. No country on the list has 6, 7, or 8, and the only 10 is Antarctica, which is not a country.

headline: Day Names
subtitle: Where do their weekday names come from?
source_name: Wikipedia, Names of the days of the week. English Sunday through Saturday are the sun, the moon, Tiw, Woden, Thor, Frigg, and Saturn. French Monday through Friday are the planets (mardi is Mars); dimanche and samedi are Lord's Day and Sabbath. Hindi names all seven for planets (Somvār, सोमवार, is the moon). Portuguese Monday through Friday are numbered ferias because Martin of Braga, archbishop of Braga (died 580), rejected the pagan names; domingo and sábado stay Lord's Day and Sabbath. Standard Chinese numbers Monday through Saturday (星期一 is week one) and Sunday is 星期日, the sun. Vietnamese numbers Monday through Saturday, and Monday, thứ hai, is second; Sunday is chủ nhật, Lord's Day. Japanese and Korean keep the seven luminaries, so Tuesday is fire: Japanese 火曜日 and Korean 화요일, the planet Mars. Greek, Russian, and Persian are left off as mixed: Greek numbers only Monday through Thursday, then Paraskevi and the Sabbath; Russian numbers only Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday; Persian numbers Sunday through Thursday from the Sabbath, and Friday is jom'e.
fun_fact: Portugal is the odd one out beside France: segunda-feira means second day, because Martin of Braga refused pagan god names and counted Monday as the second church feria, while French mardi is still Mars. India's Monday is Somvar, the moon, the same planet week as English. Vietnam also says second, thứ hai, while China's Monday is 星期一, week one, and Japan's Tuesday is 火曜日, Mars written as the element fire. Korean 화요일 is that same fire.

headline: Pepper or Bird
subtitle: Is their slang a chili pepper or a bird?
stat_label: Slang for a penis, by the word's other meaning
source_name: Royal Spanish Academy, Diccionario de la lengua española: chile is the chili and, marked vulgar for Mexico, El Salvador and Guatemala, a penis; polla is a vulgar word for a penis and also a young hen. National Institute of Korean Language, Korean Basic Dictionary, 고추: a red pepper, and figuratively a young boy's genitals. Oxford English Dictionary, cock, n.1: coarse slang for the penis, and the male bird. Treccani, uccello: a bird, and popularly the male organ. Michaelis, pinto: a young chicken, and colloquially a penis; Priberam marks that penis sense Brazilian and informal. Vietnamese Wiktionary, chim: a bird, and thông tục a penis. Badan Pengembangan dan Pembinaan Bahasa, KBBI, burung: a bird, and colloquially the male genitals. Thai Wiktionary lists phrik, พริก, as the chili plant, a jacana, and a snake, with no genital sense, so Thailand is off the board. French zizi is a childish word for a penis and does not mean a bird; coq was not entered as a penis sense. The United States uses cock as well and is not a second row.
fun_fact: Spain's polla is a young hen and the vulgar word, so it sits with Britain's cock, the male chicken. Mexico's chile is the chili pepper, and the same academy lists that as a vulgar word for a penis in Mexico. South Korea's gochu, 고추, is that pepper, and the Korean dictionary's second sense is a little boy's penis. Italy's uccello is the ordinary word for a bird. Brazil's pinto is a chick. Vietnam's chim is a bird. Indonesia's burung is a bird, and the national dictionary's colloquial sense is the male genitals.

headline: Aunt or Not
subtitle: Is the euphemism an aunt visiting?
source_name: Margot Vancauwenbergh and Karlien Franco, Women, blood, and dangerous things, Language and Cognition, 2023: Mandarin 大姨妈 'big aunt', German die rote Tante 'the red aunt', Dutch tante Rosa 'aunt Rose'. The paper's visitation example from the earlier literature is Auntie Flo. Wiktionary, Aunt Flo: a personification of menstruation, a pun on flow. French Wiktionary, les Anglais ont débarqué: familiar for the menses, cited from 1851 and 2004, from the red British coats. English Wiktionary, kommunister i lysthuset: slang for menstruation, cited from 1980, 1983 and 2016; lysthuset is a gazebo. Caldas Aulete, chico: Brazilian, vulgar, menstruation; estar com o chico means to be menstruating. Japanese Wikipedia, 月経, citing Suzuki Akiko, おんなの身体論 (Iwata Shoin, 2018), p. 47, for 月のもの as a traditional name. Norway, and a South African granny or aunt, were not found in a dictionary. Tante Rosa is the Dutch phrase in the 2023 study, so it is not the German row.
fun_fact: China's 大姨妈 means big aunt, and the Netherlands says tante Rosa, Aunt Rose, so both are a visit. Germany's phrase is die rote Tante, the red aunt. The United States says Aunt Flo, and Flo is a pun on flow. France says les Anglais ont débarqué, the English have landed, because the coats were red. Denmark says kommunister i lysthuset, communists in the gazebo. Brazil says estar com o chico, which the dictionary defines as menstruating. Japan's 月のもの is the moon's thing, a name for the monthly cycle.

headline: Language Families
subtitle: Which family is their main language in?
stat_label: Family of the main or state language
source_name: Glottolog: German and Persian are Indo-European, Hungarian, Finnish and Estonian are Uralic, Turkish and Kazakh are Turkic, and Khalkha Mongolian is Mongolic. Mongolic is its own family, not a branch of Turkic. Wikipedia, Kazakh alphabets: Cyrillic is the script used in Kazakhstan; a 2017 decree ordered a Latin alphabet and in 2021 the deadline moved to 2031. Wikipedia, Mongolian Cyrillic alphabet: the script used for Mongolian in Mongolia. Persian is written in a Perso-Arabic alphabet. Vietnamese is Austroasiatic and Maltese is Semitic, inside Afroasiatic; both use the Latin alphabet and are named only in the fact.
fun_fact: Iran sorts with Germany because Persian is Indo-European, written in the Arabic script, while Arabic is Semitic. Hungary, Finland and Estonia are Uralic, beside Indo-European neighbors. Turkish and Kazakh are both Turkic, and Kazakh is still mainly written in Cyrillic, so it looks Slavic. Mongolia writes Mongolian in Cyrillic too, and Mongolian is Mongolic, so the script is the trap: it is not Slavic, and it is not Turkic like Kazakh. Vietnam's Latin letters are Austroasiatic, and Malta's are Afroasiatic, the same alphabet trap, and neither is on this board.
